historical_timeline.summary: Born in Vinci (or nearby Anchiano, by tradition), son of a notary and a woman named Caterina.
Left-handed drawing and mirror writing documented from his early twenties.
Vasari's account of his strong right hand; an engraving shows him playing the lira da braccio.
Settles at Clos Lucé, Amboise, at the King's invitation.
A visiting cardinal's secretary records a paralysis of his right hand; he still draws and teaches.
Dies at Clos Lucé, aged 67, after an illness of some months by Vasari's account.
Retrospective proposals of stroke, ulnar or median nerve palsy, ADHD, and dyslexia; all disputed or possible.

claims.statement: A note by his grandfather Antonio records that his grandson, son of Ser Piero, was born on Saturday 15 April [1452] at the third hour of the night (Julian calendar; 24 April 1452 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar). The museums of Vinci read the note as placing his birth in Vinci itself; a long tradition places it in a farmhouse at nearby Anchiano.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The birthplace within the Vinci area is uncertain: Vinci by the grandfather's note, Anchiano by tradition.

claims.statement: He was the son of Ser Piero da Vinci, a notary, and a woman named Caterina; a land-office return of 1458 lists 'Lionardo son of the said Ser Piero, not legitimate, born of him and Chaterina'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history; the health and causes of death of his parents are not recorded in the cited sources.

claims.statement: He was left-handed: the shading and hatching of his drawings slope from upper left to lower right, and his private notes, from his early twenties onward, are written in mirror script with the left hand. A review of the documents concluded that he used his right hand for work other than drawing and writing, and it has been claimed that he never painted with his left hand.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His left-handed drawing and mirror writing are well documented; which hand he painted with is debated.

claims.statement: The biographer Giorgio Vasari wrote that he was physically so strong that with his right hand he could bend the ring of an iron door knocker or a horseshoe as if they were lead; an engraving of about 1505 shows him playing the lira da braccio.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A sixteenth-century biographer's account; it suggests his right hand worked well into his fifties.

claims.statement: At the invitation of King Francis I, who called him 'my father', he settled at the Château du Clos Lucé, at Amboise, in the autumn of 1516.

On 10 October 1517 (Julian; 20 October, Gregorian) he received Cardinal Luigi d'Aragona at Clos Lucé and showed him his paintings, among them a Florentine lady painted from life. The cardinal's secretary, Antonio de Beatis, wrote in his diary that no more good work could be expected of him 'as a certain paralysis has crippled his right hand', and that although he could no longer paint with the sweetness that was peculiar to him, 'he can still design and instruct others'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An eyewitness diary records weakness of the right hand without its cause, onset, or other signs; he continued to draw and teach.

claims.statement: His late work includes drawings of the Deluge, of cats, horses, and dragons, of water, of machines, and anatomical studies, which scholars take as evidence that his left-handed drawing was unimpaired.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The dating of individual late drawings is not given in the source.

claims.statement: On 23 April 1519 (Julian) he made his will, leaving his manuscripts and drawings to his pupil Francesco Melzi, and he died in his bed at Clos Lucé on 2 May 1519 (Julian; 12 May 1519, Gregorian), aged 67.
Vasari wrote that, having grown old, he remained ill for many months, and that he died after a paroxysm, the 'messenger of death', in the arms of the King.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Vasari's account is the only description of his death; the scene in the King's arms is a biographer's report, and the nature of the final illness is not known.

claims.statement: Several physicians have interpreted the paralysis of his right hand as the result of a stroke: a 2007 review listed a probable stroke with paralysis of the right arm and unimpaired speech; a 2019 essay described a severe left-hemisphere stroke at 65; and a 2009 paper related the stroke to a vegetarian diet.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretations; no source describes sudden onset, facial weakness, or loss of speech.

claims.statement: In 2019 Lazzeri and Rossi argued from a sixteenth-century red-chalk portrait attributed to Giovan Ambrogio Figino, which shows his right arm in folds of clothing like a bandage and the hand in a stiff, contracted position, that the hand does not show the clenched spasticity of stroke and that an ulnar nerve palsy (claw hand), most likely after an acute injury, is more plausible; they also raised focal dystonia, and judged Dupuytren's disease unlikely.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective hypothesis from a portrait; the modern episode uses ulnar neuropathy as its teaching diagnosis without asserting it historically.

claims.statement: In reply, de Campos and colleagues argued that the hand in the Figino drawing is in the 'hand of benediction' position of a median nerve injury, not the claw hand of an ulnar palsy.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A competing retrospective reading of the same portrait.

claims.statement: In 2019 Catani and Mazzarello proposed that attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder might explain his lifelong procrastination and difficulty finishing works, and noted that his mirror writing and spelling errors have been considered suggestive of dyslexia.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective speculation; not used as a diagnosis in this record.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate new weakness, numbness, and clawing of the right hand in a 65-year-old left-handed artist after a fall onto the elbow: localize the lesion by examination (ulnar sensory split of the ring finger, dorsal ulnar sensory loss, intrinsic and deep flexor weakness, Froment and Wartenberg signs, Tinel and elbow flexion tests) and keep stroke in the differential, excluded by a normal neurological examination and brain MRI; elbow X-ray for fracture; nerve conduction studies and EMG to AANEM criteria and nerve ultrasound to confirm ulnar neuropathy at the elbow and exclude C8 radiculopathy and plexopathy; conservative care (night splint, elbow pad, avoiding pressure and prolonged flexion, hand therapy with an anti-claw splint and adapted tools) and a shared decision on surgery (in situ decompression, transposition, or later tendon transfers) following AAOS guidance and the Cochrane review; keeping him working with his dominant left hand; and a stroke risk-factor screen (blood pressure, lipids, HbA1c, and an ECG for atrial fibrillation) with a shared decision on a statin.

hpi.narrative: Mr. da Vinci returns two weeks after his first visit, six weeks after he slipped on the stone stairs and landed on his bent right elbow. The numbness of the little finger and the inner half of the ring finger and the weakness of the right hand are unchanged; the ring and little fingers still curl when he opens his hand, and he cannot hold the palette or a fine brush. Elbow pain has eased with acetaminophen. He has used a towel around the elbow at night and a gel pad at the drawing table. He has had no new symptoms in the face, speech, vision, legs, or left hand. His home blood pressure readings over a week averaged 127/77 mmHg. He had nerve conduction studies, EMG, and an ultrasound this morning and saw Dr. Lindqvist-Obi of hand surgery afterwards. He draws and writes with his left hand as before.

assessment_plan.assessment: Sensory loss in the ulnar fingers and the dorsal ulnar hand, with weakness of the intrinsic muscles and the deep flexor of the little finger, localizes to the ulnar nerve at or above the elbow, not at the wrist. Nerve conduction studies show focal slowing across the elbow (36 m/s against 57 m/s in the forearm) and a 38 percent fall in amplitude, meeting AANEM criteria for ulnar neuropathy at the elbow; EMG shows active denervation in ulnar hand muscles with normal median, radial, and C8 paraspinal muscles, excluding C8 radiculopathy and lower trunk plexopathy. Ultrasound shows a swollen nerve at the medial epicondyle with no ganglion or subluxation. The elbow X-ray showed no fracture. A stroke is excluded: the weakness follows one peripheral nerve, the rest of the neurological examination is normal, and the MRI of the brain showed no infarct. Severity is moderate to severe, with some axonal loss
plan: Night elbow splint and daytime anti-claw splint, fitted in the clinic today
Hand therapy twice a week: strength, dexterity, and adapted tools for painting
No corticosteroid injection

Conservative treatment for about three months from the injury, with grip, pinch, and two-point discrimination at each review; surgery to be discussed if strength does not improve, as Dr. Lindqvist-Obi advises

referral.question: Four weeks of numbness of the ulnar fingers, weakness, and clawing of the right hand after a fall onto the bent elbow in a 65-year-old left-handed artist who paints with the right hand. Stroke has been excluded by examination and MRI. Please confirm the site and severity with nerve studies and ultrasound and advise on splinting, hand therapy, and surgery
referral.urgency: Soon, within two weeks; motor weakness with early wasting
referral.pertinent_history: Mr. da Vinci is a 65-year-old painter, engineer, and teacher who draws and writes with his left hand and holds the palette and does much of his brushwork with his right. Four weeks ago he slipped on stone stairs and landed on his bent right elbow; within two days the little finger and the inner half of the ring finger went numb, and the hand became weak, with curling of the ring and little fingers. He cannot hold the palette or a fine brush and drops small objects. Symptoms are worse when he leans on the elbow at his drawing table and at night. He has no neck pain and no face, speech, vision, leg, or left-hand symptoms, and the onset was not sudden. On examination there is sensory loss over the little finger, the ulnar half of the ring finger, and the dorsal ulnar hand; the first dorsal interosseous and abductor digiti minimi are 3/5 and the deep flexor of the little finger 4/5, with positive Froment and Wartenberg signs, mild clawing, and early first web wasting; thumb abduction and wrist and finger extension are normal; Tinel and elbow flexion tests are positive at the cubital tunnel. The rest of the neurological examination is normal (NIH Stroke Scale 0). Same-day MRI of the brain showed no infarct, the elbow X-ray showed no fracture, and the ECG showed sinus rhythm. Blood count, metabolic panel, HbA1c, TSH, vitamin B12, and lipids were sent. He uses a towel around the elbow at night and acetaminophen for pain. He is anxious to keep working
questions: Do nerve conduction studies, EMG, and ultrasound confirm ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, and do they exclude a C8 radiculopathy, plexopathy, or a lesion at the wrist?
How severe is it, and is there axonal loss?
Which splints and hand therapy do you advise, and is a corticosteroid injection useful?
Should he have surgery now or after a trial of conservative treatment, and when should that decision be made?
If surgery is needed, which procedure, and what is the place of tendon transfers for the claw?
How can he keep working, with his left hand and with adapted tools?

consultant_note.history: Mr. da Vinci is seen at the request of Dr. Carrow-Asante, six weeks after he fell onto his bent right elbow on stone stairs. Numbness of the little finger and inner ring finger began within two days, followed by weakness and curling of the ring and little fingers. He is left-handed for drawing and writing but uses the right hand to hold the palette and for brushwork on large panels, and he leans on his elbows for hours at a drawing table. Symptoms have not changed in two weeks of avoiding pressure on the elbow. He has had no previous elbow injury, neck pain, or symptoms in the other hand. He has no diabetes, and he does not smoke
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Today's nerve conduction studies: right ulnar motor conduction velocity 36 m/s across the elbow against 57 m/s in the forearm, a 38 percent fall in compound muscle action potential amplitude across the elbow, and reduced right ulnar sensory and dorsal ulnar cutaneous responses; median, radial, and left ulnar studies normal. Needle EMG: fibrillation potentials and reduced recruitment in the first dorsal interosseous and abductor digiti minimi, milder changes in the deep flexor of the little finger, normal flexor carpi ulnaris, abductor pollicis brevis, extensor indicis, and C8 paraspinal muscles. Ultrasound: ulnar nerve cross-sectional area 14 mm2 at the medial epicondyle against 7 mm2 in the forearm, no subluxation, no ganglion or mass. MRI of the brain (no infarct), X-ray of the elbow (no fracture; small medial osteophyte), and ECG (sinus rhythm) from the first visit

assessment.assessment: Moderately severe ulnar neuropathy at the elbow after a blow to the nerve at the cubital tunnel, with partial conduction block, focal demyelination, and some axonal loss (active denervation in the hand muscles). The studies meet AANEM criteria for localization at the elbow and exclude a lesion at the wrist, a C8 radiculopathy, and a lower trunk plexopathy. The nerve does not sublux, and there is no fracture, ganglion, or mass. Because the injury was acute and part of the deficit is conduction block, some recovery with protection of the nerve is likely, but the axonal loss and early wasting mean that recovery may be incomplete

recommendations: Conservative treatment for about three months from the injury: a night splint holding the elbow at about 45 degrees, a gel elbow pad, no leaning on the elbow, and no prolonged elbow bending

A daytime hand-based anti-claw splint for the ring and little fingers to improve grasp, and hand therapy twice a week for strength, dexterity, and adapted tools: built-up brush handles, a lighter brush, and a palette fixed to the easel
No corticosteroid injection, which the Cochrane review found no better than placebo

Review at about three months from the injury with grip, pinch, two-point discrimination, and the QuickDASH; if motor strength has not clearly improved, or if weakness or wasting progress at any time, I would advise surgery rather than waiting longer

If surgery is needed, in situ decompression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow, which the Cochrane review found as effective as transposition with fewer wound infections; anterior transposition only if the nerve subluxes at operation. Repeat nerve studies are not needed before surgery unless the picture changes
Tendon transfers to correct the claw only if it persists a year or more after decompression
He should keep drawing, writing, and teaching with his left hand without restriction, and paint with the adapted tools and help with heavy or prolonged right-hand tasks
